Through a systematic search, the data was collected from major databases from 2012 to 2021 across major academic and open-access databases, including Google Scholar, PubMed, JSTOR, Web of Science, Sage Journals, and Library Genesis. Out of an initial pool of 172 potentially relevant research articles, the researchers identified and selected 135 articles that were most directly related to their specific research topic sexual violence against women for an in-depth, systematic review. The review indicates that sensational reporting remains more prevalent than responsible reporting across many cultural contexts, although important regional differences were identified.

latest.title: Ten years of the mobile world congress: Media impact on the city of Barcelona
latest.abstract: The Mobile World Congress (MWC) has become an international benchmark in mobile technology and one of the most significant events hosted in Barcelona. Beyond its technological relevance, its media visibility may have played a key role in shaping the city’s public image and international reputation. This study aims to examine the impact of media coverage of the Mobile World Congress on the promotion and positioning of the city of Barcelona. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining content analysis and sentiment analysis through the implementation of a hierarchical multiclass automatic classification system. The study analysed news coverage published in three major regional newspapers— La Vanguardia , Ara.Cat , and El Periódico ( n = 3523 news articles). This methodological design enabled the identification of thematic patterns, dominant narratives, and the frequency with which Barcelona was associated with the event. The findings indicate that media coverage of the MWC has had a notably positive effect on Barcelona’s visibility and reputation. The newspapers consistently presented the city as a leading hub for technological innovation, international business, and large-scale global events. Recurrent references to Barcelona’s organisational capacity and strategic relevance within the mobile technology sector contributed to strengthening its urban brand and enhancing its symbolic capital in both regional and international media discourse. The MWC has significantly contributed to boosting and promoting the city of Barcelona. Media representation of the event has reinforced the city’s status as a global, innovation-driven urban centre and has consolidated its position within the international technological landscape.

latest.title: Feeling the crisis, building the alternative: Women journalists in nonprofit digital media through the lens of feminist epistemology and the affective turn
latest.abstract: This article draws on feminist standpoint epistemology and the affective turn to examine how women journalists respond to deteriorating working conditions in Slovenian legacy media. The study focuses on three analytically selected cases of women journalists who co-founded nonprofit, women-led digital media outlets, drawn from 15 exploratory autobiographical interviews. Their narratives articulate experiences of marginalization alongside agentic responses that critically interrogate developments in the legacy media system and call for a rethinking of journalistic ethics and labor organization. Journalism is approached as affective labor, marked by the entanglement of passion, self-exploitation, and precarity, in which emotions such as anger, care, and responsibility – combined with digital affordances – enable the creation of alternative media spaces. These initiatives are interpreted not merely as individual survival strategies but as micropolitical and epistemological interventions that reclaim professional autonomy and integrity. While embedded in neoliberal conditions and structurally fragile, they demonstrate the potential of alternative practices to reimagine journalism from the margins.

latest.title: Affective journalism and identity: Community newspapers as emotional agents in Hong Kong
latest.abstract: Situated within Hong Kong’s rapidly shifting sociopolitical context and complex identity landscape, this article examines how community newspapers produce community imaginaries in Hong Kong, focusing on the affective-discursive strategies through which grassroots journalism constructs community knowledge. Treating emotion as an epistemic infrastructure, this article draws on affective epistemology to examine how such strategies in two ideologically divergent community newspapers constitute distinct forms of community knowledge for readers. Through a comparative critical discourse analysis of one pro-democracy and one pro-establishment community newspaper, the analysis identifies two distinct affective strategies: an affective-participatory strategy that constitutes community as a self-determining collective subject, and an affective-governance strategy that constitutes community as a condition of harmony sustained through virtuous individuals and aligned institutions.

latest.title: When journalists and scientists sit down to talk: Juggling audience expectations in interactional science podcasts during the COVID-19 pandemic
latest.abstract: Given the growing relevance of podcasts in science communication, especially science journalism, this paper analyzes interactional science podcasts from a dramaturgical perspective. Scientists and journalists face conflicting expectations from different audiences, ranging from professional peers to a ‘general audience.’ Nevertheless, their interactions tend to be relatively harmonious. This paper addresses this puzzle and asks how journalists and scientists juggle audience expectations in different roles. It is based on a qualitative analysis of 15 episodes of the prominent German podcast ‘Coronavirus Update,’ sampled through mentions in metajournalistic discourse during the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany. The analysis shows that conflicting expectations require a certain variation within role constellations: actors speak as (co-)moderator, (co-)expert, and as a representative of the audience. The constellations are stabilized through mutual support of each other’s self-presentation, but also the intentional withdrawal thereof in risky situations. Unpacking those interactional dynamics, shaped by audience expectations, helps to understand the social dimension of science journalism and its emerging practices, such as podcasting.

latest.title: Institutional realism in media culture: How disability journalism education reveals structural limits of cultural change
latest.abstract: Media institutions systematically exclude disability perspectives despite decades of advocacy and educational intervention. This article examines why cultural transformation efforts fail to penetrate professional media practice, extending Mark Fisher’s concept of ‘capitalist realism’ to reveal how institutional realism operates: we can imagine transformed practitioners but not transformed institutions. Drawing on critical autoethnographic analysis of two contrasting disability reporting education initiatives, an intensive community-partnered program and widely-distributed industry guidance, I demonstrate how professional socialisation functions as a mechanism of cultural reproduction, systematically neutralising educational gains through reification processes. While both interventions demonstrably transformed individual practitioners, neither disrupted what Jacques Rancière (2004) terms the ‘distribution of the sensible’ that determines whose voices become audible in media discourse. This case contributes to critical theory by specifying how institutional realism lets institutions appear to embrace cultural change while containing it. The analysis reveals a depth-versus-scale paradox: interventions intensive enough to transform how practitioners see disability cannot be scaled, while interventions that scale reach only those already disposed to change. It specifies two frameworks: the distinction between epistemic transformation and behavioural modification, and the mechanism through which newsroom routines reify ableist assumptions as professional competence, and positional disability expertise as optional specialisation rather than core.

latest.title: The meaning and viability of redress: How newspapers and polls frame reparations
latest.abstract: Despite reparations for slavery being part of the historical struggle for racial justice in the United States, the issue has fallen at the periphery of political discourse. Yet, in 2019 and 2020, the news devoted substantially more attention to the issue as Democratic primary candidates discussed it in debates and it was championed by the Movement for Black Lives. However, despite the fact we know that coverage increased during this time, we know surprisingly little about how reparations were discussed. This study analyzes the framing decisions present in opinion pieces across three of the largest U.S. national newspapers—and how these decisions interacted with public opinion polling and general election coverage in 2019 and 2020. I find that reparations were commonly discussed without mentioning any specific form. Instead, the issue framed as one of many radical and unpopular issues championed by people on the far left before the 2020 election.

latest.title: The polarized talk least about polarization: Polarization discourses in tabloids and broadsheets from UK, Germany and Sweden
latest.abstract: This study examines how newspapers from three distinct national contexts—the UK, Germany, and Sweden—report about polarization, and how such coverage makes societal division visible and emotionally salient. Drawing on 230,000 news articles from 2014 to 2023, we use Word2Vec, Named Entity Recognition, topic modeling, and anger classification to identify and analyze journalistic metadiscourse about polarization and broader division. Across countries and outlets, references to polarization increased markedly during the decade. Sweden, the least polarized country in our comparison, showed the highest volume of polarization discourse. Tabloids generally feature higher levels of anger in broader coverage but report less often about polarization than broadsheets. These findings are consistent with a reflexive-journalism logic, whereby polarization discourse is most frequent in outlets that interpret and contextualize broader societal developments, rather than in the most polarized settings. The study highlights the need for cross-national perspectives on how media frame and write about societal division.

latest.title: Anchored in capital: A Bourdieusian analysis of journalistic identity and resilience in the Portuguese field
latest.abstract: This repeated cross-sectional study (2013-2023) examines the resilience of professional values in Portuguese journalism amid economic precarity and digital disruption. Integrating Bourdieu’s field theory with Raemy’s multi-level identity model, we show how journalists reinforce symbolic capital—intensifying watchdog roles and ethical norms—to preserve field autonomy. Using data from two waves of the Worlds of Journalism Study-Portugal, we analyze how this defensive consolidation operates through capital conversion across macro, meso, and micro levels. The findings reframe value stability not as inertia but as active identity work, offering insights into how peripheral media systems sustain professional coherence under duress.

latest.title: Stigma, erasure, and change: Newspaper coverage of prostitution in the mid-20th century
latest.abstract: This project studied news articles about prostitution in the mid-century U.S. to explore the impact of second wave feminism on coverage. Based on a content analysis of 630 articles downloaded from Newspapers.com from the 1950s, ‘60s and ‘70s, it found that while patriarchal values dominated coverage overall, changes could be discerned in the 1970s. Typically, women’s voices were linguistically marginalized even when they were included in coverage. Men, whether as news reporters or as members of law enforcement, were usually the framers of such stories, and when women were included, they were rarely named and quoted far less often. Yet as more women wrote news in the 1970s, stories reflected more concern for women involved in prostitution and were more likely to include their voice. The findings contribute to feminist scholarship and studies of the history of news by underscoring how such coverage, reflected, reinforced, or challenged broader societal hierarchies and power dynamics.

latest.title: “X is simply broken”: The relationship between political journalists and politicians on social media during the 2025 German federal election campaign
latest.abstract: Contemporary election campaigns are marked by a move from political parties and politicians to communicating directly to audiences via social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and TikTok. In doing so, they deliberately bypass journalistic rigour and scrutiny to focus on more personal messages and storytelling techniques. Scholarship has investigated this from the perspective of social media platform logics and political campaigning but has thus far somewhat neglected the journalistic dimension. Using the case study of the snap German federal elections held in February 2025, this contribution features expert interviews with a diverse range of German political journalists and investigates their perspectives on a) how leading politicians used social media platforms in their campaigns and b) how they use said platforms themselves for news sourcing and diffusion as well as direct communication with politicians. Findings reveal a shift away from X (formerly Twitter) and a stronger focus on more outspoken audiovisual platforms such as TikTok for news sourcing and diffusion purposes, while ascribing growing relevance to LinkedIn and even traditional text messages. Politicians’ messages are perceived as steering away from overt political messages, feeding into the ongoing debate about the depoliticization of political communication.

latest.title: The power of conversational writing style: Examining the influence of sourcing and writing style on credibility in community journalism
latest.abstract: This article revisits the issue of the credibility of citizen journalism in the context of community news. By unpacking its two major reporting characteristics — sourcing from citizens and conversational writing style — this study contributes to our understanding of what makes citizen journalism trustworthy. A 2 (sourcing: elite vs citizen) × 2 (writing style: conversational vs professional) between-subjects experiment ( N = 311) was conducted in Taiwan in late January 2024. Results showed that conversational writing style was considered more credible and more narratively transported than professional journalistic writing. Besides, media skepticism moderated the relationship between conversational writing style and narrative transportation. This implies that, at least concerning community topics, conversational writing style emerges as the critical factor enabling citizen journalism to win trust among the public. Furthermore, results suggest a need to reconsider the rigid professional journalistic norms in certain settings, as the traditional reporting style creates a distance with readers and may be unsuitable for addressing personal-related or emotionally charged topics such as community news and disaster news.

latest.title: Being journalists on social media: Contrasting professionals’ self-perceptions to role expectations among adolescents
latest.abstract: On social media, efforts by individual journalists to share news with audiences may be a viable response to personality-driven news presentation coming from peripheral actors like influencers, who are increasingly popular information sources for adolescents. Yet, when using social media to disseminate content, journalists may risk backlash, especially when innovative approaches represent a deviation from traditional journalistic norms. Drawing on expectancy violations theory and semi-structured qualitative interviews conducted among Portuguese journalists ( N = 7) and adolescents ( N = 20), we contrasted professionals’ own perceptions of being journalists on social media to adolescents’ role expectations. Findings showed that adolescents generally prefer journalists to be personal and independent when presenting news on social media, though they also recognized that journalists may in this context be bound by institutional rules. Similarly, journalists highlighted perceived pressure coming from news organizations and licensing bodies to abide by professional standards, even when using their private social media. Despite seeing value in adopting a ‘newsfluencer’-like role, journalists’ need to negotiate between various interests and expectations represents one of the main hurdles that prevents them from establishing a clear presence on these platforms – and may explain low attraction to journalistic sources on social media among adolescents.

latest.title: When even empathy would be enough – Representation of homelessness in the Czech mainstream media during Christmas
latest.abstract: Homelessness remains one of the most persistent and complex societal issues globally, and the media play a significant role in shaping both representations of and public attitudes toward this marginalized population. This study presents a thematic analysis of Czech mainstream news coverage of homelessness during three consecutive Christmas periods (2022, 2023, and 2024). While Christmas coverage might be expected to foreground empathy, humanization, or solidarity more strongly than routine reporting, the analysis shows that such elements remained relatively marginal in the Czech material examined here. The findings reveal a persistent scarcity of solidarity and empathy, with media portrayals frequently reinforcing harmful stereotypes rather than challenging them. The study concludes that substantial changes in media discourse are necessary to promote more accurate and just representations of homelessness in the Czech and possibly further Eastern European context.

latest.title: Framing the regional frontlines: challenges, ethical dilemmas and experiences of Journalists in Northeast India
latest.abstract: This article investigates how journalists in Northeast India negotiate objectivity, ethics and journalistic role perceptions while covering conflicts in geo-politically sensitive and digitally mediated settings. Drawing on eight in-depth interviews, this study reveals how journalists navigate safety concerns, emotional connections and platform logics that increasingly affect their workflows. Employing Framing Theory and Role Theory, the paper highlights three interconnected dimensions: journalists’ reflexive negotiation between emotional attachment and professional neutrality, increasing influence of platform logics and analytics in editorial processes; and contextual restrictions arising from state control and linguistic hegemonies within the Indian national media landscape. The findings demonstrate that in conflict settings, journalistic objectivity is contextually negotiated rather than being universally fixed, highlighting moral sensitivities and hybrid professionalism in peripheral media settings. By examining the lived realities of journalists; the study contributes to de-Westernised discourses in Journalism Studies and explains how journalists in parts of the Global South, especially in conflict-sensitive and marginalised territories, reimagine journalistic ethics and agency amid political, cultural and technological challenges.

latest.title: From “water, food, energy” to electoral legitimacy: media discourse and symbolic meaning-making in Romania’s 2024 election crisis
latest.abstract: This article examines how populist political legitimacy is discursively constructed through semiotic framing in a context of democratic instability. Focusing on Romania’s 2024 presidential crisis, the study analyses how nationalist and anti-establishment meanings are produced, circulated, and recontextualized across digital and traditional media environments. Drawing on semiotic theory and critical discourse approaches, the article explores how recurring symbolic elements, such as sovereignty , moral purity , and elemental resources , operate as indexical signs that connect individual grievances to broader ideological narratives. The analysis combines qualitative discourse analysis of candidate communication, computational analysis of 10,556 news articles, and post-electoral survey data ( N = 572) collected immediately after the first round of voting. The analysis shows how discursive strategies contribute to processes of political legitimation by framing power relations in affective and moral terms rather than procedural or institutional ones. Empirical survey data are used to contextualize how these symbolic repertoires circulated across fragmented media environments and were associated with differentiated patterns of electoral alignment. The findings highlight the central role of media discourse and symbolic framing in shaping political legitimacy, polarization, and interpretive authority within contemporary hybrid media systems, offering insights into the symbolic mechanisms through which legitimacy is negotiated in post-socialist societies.

latest.title: Epistemic governance in journalism: Editorial, algorithmic, and regulatory logics in a contested epistemic space
latest.abstract: Journalism’s epistemic authority—its capacity to produce and legitimate public knowledge—is shaped beyond the newsroom. Editorial judgment now operates alongside algorithmic systems that structure visibility and distribution, and regulatory frameworks that impose obligations and safeguards. Although scholarship has examined these domains separately, it lacks an integrated account of how epistemic authority is enacted across them. This article develops an Epistemic Governance Framework that conceptualizes journalism’s authority as a governed outcome of three interdependent logics: editorial, algorithmic, and regulatory. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory, the article treats these logics as overlapping sociotechnical arrangements and proposes their intersection as a Contested Epistemic Space in which competing criteria of visibility, credibility, and accountability are negotiated. The article contributes a framework for analyzing how journalistic authority is assembled, contested, and stabilized, and outlines implications for future empirical research and normative debate on the governance of public knowledge.

latest.title: Reporting the periphery: War and peace journalism in the coverage of the 2023 Manipur violence
latest.abstract: This study examines national media coverage of ethnic conflict through the lens of peace journalism, focusing on the 2023 Manipur conflict in Northeast India – a region often absent from national news discourse. While peace journalism research has expanded across diverse conflict contexts, scholarship foregrounding marginalized peripheral regions remains limited. Drawing on Galtung’s peace journalism framework and center-periphery theory as complementary analytical lenses, the study analyzed 360 news reports published by three leading Indian national news outlets from May to October 2023. The analysis identified the prevalence of war and peace frames across outlets and employed a novel indicator co-occurrence approach to assess the depth of violence coverage. Results show a clear dominance of war frames, with emphasis on immediate developments, visible effects of violence, and elite sources, while peace-oriented indicators such as the examination of causes, civilian voices, and solution orientation were systematically underrepresented. An indicator-level analysis further revealed that while outlets diverge in framing orientation and language use, they converge in their failure to engage with contextual depth. A key implication is that journalistic neutrality alone does not necessarily prevent, and may inadvertently contribute to, the epistemic marginalization of peripheral communities in national conflict reporting.

latest.title: “This is how journalism has always been done”: White neutrality, newsroom norms, and an AI intervention in source diversification
latest.abstract: This study draws on interviews with 12 journalists in a Canadian newsroom to examine how they understand source diversification, how they perceive AI-based source-tracking technology, and how their reflections illuminate discourse on race and accountability in journalism. Based on semi-structured interviews conducted after a demonstration of the technology, the analysis identifies the motivations and barriers shaping source diversification, including professional norms, representational goals, time constraints, and institutional culture. Reporters express commitments to inclusive sourcing, but remain constrained by routines that privilege official voices, anticipated by research analysis like framing and indexing theories. Participants describe the AI tool, which quantitatively scores sources according to their relationship to societal power structures, as a potential catalyst for reflective practice and accountability. They also suggest the technology may sit uneasily within professional norms. The study is contextualized in research about role performance and race in newsrooms. Finally, this AI-based source-tracking technology resituates journalism within a Bourdieusian field, pulled toward social and cultural capital in relation to structural racism.

latest.title: “Talk as if it doesn’t impact you”: Black TV journalist’s experiences covering BLM protests in the U.S.
latest.abstract: This article explores the effects that covering Black Lives Matter protests had on Black TV journalists. Using in-depth semi-structured interviews with 14 Black journalists across the U.S., this study investigates their experiences covering BLM protests, as well as how supported they felt by their organizations/supervisors. Through qualitative interviews, research shows that Black journalists felt torn between their identities as both journalists and Black—navigating objective reporting with a deep emotional empathy for protestors. Moreover, they did not feel supported by their news organizations, who did not prioritize their well-being, and who tailored news coverage for a White audience. The intersectional implications of this are discussed as well as concerns about emotional labor.

latest.title: Investigating under fire: Journalistic challenges in Afghanistan’s Republic era (2001–2021)
latest.abstract: Investigative journalism plays a vital role in exposing wrongdoing. This study examines the practices and challenges of investigative reporting in Afghanistan during the Republic era (2001–2021). Drawing on in-depth interviews with fifteen investigative journalists from leading television networks, it applies the Hierarchy of Influences model to analyze how multiple levels of pressure shaped investigative reporting in a conflict-affected context. The findings reveal that investigative reporting was constrained across the individual, routines, organizational, extramedia, and social system levels. At the individual level, journalists engaged in anticipatory self-censorship. At the routines level, newsroom practices and narration strategies reflected the normalization of insecurity in everyday work. Organizational pressures, including financial constraints, media dependency, and editorial control, undermined investigative practice. At the extramedia level, pressures from government officials, armed groups, and other actors created an unpredictable reporting environment. At the social system level, weak rule of law, limited enforcement, restricted access to information, and cultural norms narrowed the scope of investigative reporting. The study extends the Hierarchy of Influences model by demonstrating that macro-level pressures converged at the story-conception stage, producing temporal compression across levels of influence. At the same time, journalists exercised negotiated agency through adaptive strategies that enabled investigative journalism to persist despite severe constraints.

latest.title: Human versus AI news anchors: A survey study on audience satisfaction and the emotional connection
latest.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes widely used in the digital newsroom, AI virtual anchors have been widely accepted, leading to the alteration of the traditional model of news presentation. In this study, perceptions, satisfaction and emotional attachment of the Chinese news viewers to the AI news anchors. A questionnaire of 343 Beijing residents was collected as primary data. Frameworks like Diffusion of Innovations (DoI) and Social Construction of Technology (SCOT) have been core theoretical foundation. The findings suggest that credibility scepticism, moderate acceptance, and low emotional connectivity with AI anchors were high. The perceived authenticity and emotional connectivity had a significant correlation with the overall satisfaction of the audience, and the acceptance patterns were mediated by demographic factors. Human communicative values such as trust, emotional appeal, and responsibility proved to be the most crucial factors in determining the interests of the audience. The implications of these findings can be applied to news organizations that are planning to use AI anchors in a manner that would not compromise the credibility and trust of their audience.

latest.title: Selective appropriation and ideological framing in BBC Persian’s coverage of the Palestinian-Israeli conflict
latest.abstract: Drawing on narrative theory and the concept of “selective appropriation,” this research conducts a critical analysis of the translation practices of BBC Persian. The study analyzed the coverage of the Palestinian-Israeli conflict after the attacks of October 7, 2023. A corpus of 48 news reports originally published in English on the BBC World News website and their corresponding Persian translations were comparatively examined. The focus of the study was on the systematic use of omission, addition, substitution, and permutation strategies in the Persian translations of BBC Persian and their ideological implications. The findings demonstrated that BBC Persian engaged in narrative reframing. Throughout a sum of 198 main framing interventions, the Persian versions of the news reports were reframed to align with the presumed ideological and political sensitivities of the Persian-speaking audience. Main strategies consisted of the omission of designating Hamas as a terrorist organization and the addition of a broader geopolitical context. In addition to that, the substitution of claims with facts to assign culpability, and the permutation of the news body and headlines to shift narrative focus from human tragedy to state failure were used. The result was a “localized version” of the news reports that construct a different narrative and ideologically distinct reality from the English source texts.

latest.title: News recommendation as a process: An interdisciplinary literature review
latest.abstract: This paper investigates how different disciplines conceptualize news recommendation, addressing the challenge of fragmented knowledge in this interdisciplinary field. Through a comprehensive literature review of 476 peer-reviewed publications from 2000 to 2022, the study analyzes terminology, citation practices, and mental models in mainly computer science, communication science, and interdisciplinary research. We find distinct disciplinary terminologies and asymmetries in epistemic authority, with computer science dominating in publication volume and citations. The study identifies four mental models structuring researchers’ representations of news recommendation, ranging from system-centric technical optimization to abstract reflections on journalism. It proposes an interdisciplinary process model integrating technical and social dimensions to bridge knowledge silos and foster interdisciplinary collaboration. The paper concludes with strategies for researchers to promote interdisciplinarity, including learning other disciplinary languages and addressing power dynamics.

latest.title: Producer, interrupted: The hidden toll of being a Global South producer making documentaries for the West
latest.abstract: Transnational documentary production relies heavily on Global South producers whose labor, expertise, and local knowledge remain central to nonfiction storytelling,yet their experiences and burdens often remain overlooked within scholarship on global journalism and representation. Drawing on dependency theory, postcolonial scholarship, and affective epistemology, I foreground documentary production as a critical site where power, authority, and authorship are negotiated. This allows me to examine how labor hierarchies and material inequalities shape both production and local producers’ embodied experiences. Using in-depth interviews with nine Pakistani producers alongside autoethnographic reflections from my own experience in transnational documentary production, I show how power asymmetries marginalize local producers despite their central creative and interpretive role. The findings identify an interconnected triple burden of material, narrative, and affective dependency at play. Local producers remain dependent not only on foreign funding and distribution infrastructures, but also on Western narrative frameworks that constrain which stories are funded, legitimized, and circulated globally. These asymmetries generate affective dependency, producing moral injury among local producers navigating unequal systems of representation.

latest.title: Complicating crisis narratives: Civic embeddedness and relational trust in the Zambian news ecosystem
latest.abstract: Much of the recent academic discourse suggests journalism is in crisis due to declining revenues, reduced public trust, and digital disruptions (D’Arma et al., 2025). Zambia, however, offers a distinctive case of a proliferating media sector, growing newspaper readership, and journalists who retain strong public esteem despite material precarity (Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung, 2022; MISA Zambia, 2020; Mwimbe, 2023). Drawing on interviews with journalists, media practitioners, educators, and local leadership across Lusaka and Muchinga Province, this article examines how journalism and public information circulate across uneven urban and rural infrastructures. Findings reveal that Zambian journalism is driven by civic commitment, strong public trust, and adaptive practices. Community radio remains a central civic platform in rural areas, whilst trusted local intermediaries help relay information where direct journalistic reach is weakened by infrastructural constraints. Digital migration has encouraged content hybridity and audience engagement, with bloggers and news outlets negotiating legitimacy and symbolic power. Despite financial and logistical challenges, investigative journalism is gaining traction, supported by public appetite for accountability. Print media retains cultural authority, especially in regions with limited internet access. The study therefore argues that Zambia complicates dominant crisis narratives by showing that civic commitment, relational trust, and hybrid adaptation can sustain journalism under precarious conditions, even where labour insecurity, structural legal vulnerabilities, and territorial exclusion persist.

latest.title: Objectivity as a shield: Journalistic voice and the strategic use of quotation in Iranian newspapers
latest.abstract: This paper identifies and analyses a distinctive journalistic practice in Iranian political news reporting, termed the “projecting voice”. This practice, observed in reports from both conservative ( Kayhan ) and reformist ( Etemaad ) newspapers, involves a near-complete absence of explicit authorial/journalist opinion, where the journalist functions primarily as a conduit for the quoted statements of high-status sources. Using a discourse-analytical approach, this study argues that the “projecting voice” is not simply passive reporting, but a strategic ritual of impersonality in service of “objective” reporting. This ritual serves as a risk-management device, allowing journalists to navigate institutional pressures while creating a veneer of objectivity. This might be due to political reasons and the sensitivity around political topics and leaders. The paper concludes that this practice challenges conventional Western models of journalistic objectivity and provides a crucial case study of how professional norms are adapted in authoritarian media environments.

latest.title: “A feeling reporter, not a robotic reporter”: Empathy, emotions, resilience, and vicarious post-traumatic growth after mass shootings
latest.abstract: This study seeks to understand the experiences of journalists reporting on mass shootings. It explores the roles of empathy and emotionality and asks if normalizing them in journalism practice can strengthen resilience and promote vicarious post-traumatic growth. Although empathy and displays of emotion are not yet embraced as journalistic norms such as objectivity, all participants spoke of the importance of empathy, particularly when covering mass shootings. Interviews with 23 journalists who reported on the mass shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas provide insight into their experiences. Although some participants differed in their views of shared emotionality, empathy, resilience, and vicarious post-traumatic growth were evident.

latest.title: Sizzling spring: the construction of seasons and seasonal transitions in Australian journalism
latest.abstract: While much of humanity can insulate itself from the full impact of seasonal weather patterns, seasons remain tools for living that frame important recurrent events and thus help structure rhythms of life and, for many, livelihoods. Journalism plays a significant role in maintaining seasons as meaningful frames around, amongst other things, sports events, nature, and leisure. Such coverage has been termed seasonal journalism: recurrent content that helps structure the year and, increasingly, our relationships to a shifting climate. As past experiences lose some of their predictive power, journalism is engaging in new ways to make sense of seasons and their transitions. This article examines how five Australian news publications constructed seasons in articles published in August and September in 2023 and 2024, as these months mark the transition from winter to spring. A key takeaway is that seasonal characteristics, anomalies, transitions, and forecasts are increasingly becoming news events in their own right, rather than merely forming a backdrop for other stories. At the same time, more conventional seasonal content (such as articles about flower shows or swooping magpies) continues to appear. But even in these stories, there are tensions between anticipation and disruption, and with that, explicit or implied attempts to make sense of climatic changes. The analysis is based on 206 articles and draws on journalism studies, environmental communication and the environmental humanities.

latest.title: Beyond the degree: Entry criteria and the influence of journalism education in Nigerian news organizations’ hiring practices
latest.abstract: This study examines the criteria that Nigerian news organizations prioritize when hiring reporters and the role of journalism education in this process. Drawing on 21 interviews with newsroom editors and 70 job advertisements, the analysis distinguishes between core “ultimate criteria” shared across organizations and more flexible “adaptable criteria” that reflect organizational and individual editors’ priorities. Framed within boundary work and gatekeeping theories, the study examines how hiring serves as a central site for regulating entry into the profession and reinforcing professional norms and values. The findings highlight the persistent gap between journalism education and industry expectations and carry important implications for policy, particularly regarding proposals to mandate journalism degrees for employment. By offering insights from an understudied context, this research advances understanding of newsroom hiring practices, the negotiation of professional boundaries, and the alignment of journalism education with industry needs in Nigeria.

latest.title: Humility in journalism: The epistemic virtue that allows journalists to learn from experiences of others
latest.abstract: Journalists have long been associated with a strong ego and the hubris necessary to share the news as “the way it is.” But overlooked, and perhaps more important, is the humility required by journalists to gather new knowledge in the first place. Through the lens of joy and journalistic epistemology, the present study explores interviews with 27 journalists in Chile and the United States in regards to their experiences with humility. Journalists broadly believed that their work could be done without humility, but that good journalism necessitated humility. The best journalists, across these national contexts, were considered to be those who were humble: which journalists defined as being willing to listen, to learn, to be corrected and to apologize for mistakes.

latest.title: Value-motivated use of generative AI among student journalists: Practices and risk management in college newsrooms
latest.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has rapidly entered journalistic practice, prompting growing scholarly attention to future journalists, particularly journalism students, and their attitudes and beliefs about its use. However, little research has examined how student journalists working in college newsrooms actually use GenAI in practice, or how they navigate its associated risks while upholding journalistic values. To address this gap, we conducted interviews with 20 student journalists working in college newsrooms. Our findings show that student journalists engage in value-motivated uses of GenAI, while also approaching the technology with caution. They actively navigate ethical concerns related to accuracy, transparency, accountability, and professional autonomy, and develop strategies to manage the risks that GenAI introduces into journalistic work. Our findings offer important theoretical contributions to understanding value-motivated uses of GenAI and perceptions of its associated risks. Our findings also provide practical implications for journalism education by informing how student journalists who represent the next generation of professionals can be better prepared to navigate an AI-mediated news environment.

latest.title: Pseudo-journalistic political communication: The Flemish far right and the appropriation of journalism for political communication ends
latest.abstract: The borders between journalism and politics have become increasingly blurry within the hybrid media system in which older and newer media logics as well as media and political logics interact in complex ways. This article examines an underexplored aspect of this evolving landscape: the appropriation of journalism for political communication ends by political parties, a phenomenon we call ‘pseudo-journalistic political communication’. With the far right having emerged as a key player in this hybridization, we examine the Belgian Vlaams Belang’s (Flemish Interest, VB) pseudo-journalistic political communication through a multimodal textual analysis of the VB ‘talk show’ VBTV and the VB-produced but seemingly independent ‘news website’ V-NIEUWS. Building on Ekman and Widholm’s (2024a) work, our study focuses on the combination of political communication logics and journalistic logics across four dimensions: (1) transparency concerning partisanship; (2) platforms used for dissemination; (3) journalistic genres and roles; and (4) discourse about journalism. Our findings highlight the party’s aptitude in drawing on journalistic logics for political communication ends but also the difficulties it faces in navigating the tensions between journalistic and political logics, particularly in formats that are more profoundly pseudo-journalistic. The conclusion builds on the comparison of V-NIEUWS and VBTV to refine the conceptualization of pseudo-journalistic political communication as one specific articulation of journalism into political communication. We also situate this phenomenon within the broader landscape of the far right’s multi-faceted engagement with journalism.

latest.title: Toward an inclusive model of journalism education: Exploring factors shaping the classroom experience of a visually impaired instructor
latest.abstract: Diversity, equity, and inclusion of visually impaired educators remain underexplored, particularly in fields that are heavily visually oriented, such as media and journalism. Drawing on the perspectives of 24 sighted journalism students in Egypt, this study investigates the factors that shape the classroom experience of a blind instructor, focusing on the interplay between pedagogical practices, student engagement, and institutional support. Using data collected through electronic interviews, the research examines how these dynamics influence student perceptions of competence, collaboration, and inclusion, as well as their broader attitudes toward disability. Findings highlight the complex relational and institutional processes that contribute to effective inclusion. Students’ engagement, combined with adaptive teaching strategies and systemic support, facilitated an environment in which disability was decoupled from assumptions of incompetence, allowing professional capabilities to be foregrounded. The study situates these insights within the framework of critical disability studies, emphasizing the social and structural dimensions of inclusion rather than framing success as an individual achievement. By conceptualizing inclusive pedagogy as a dynamic, multi-stakeholder process, this research offers a model for integrating visually impaired educators in visually oriented disciplines and contributes to broader discussions on dismantling ableist norms and fostering equitable academic environments.

latest.title: Infrastructures of listening: AI and the reconfiguration of community-centered newswork
latest.abstract: This study examines how AI-supported tools can reshape journalistic epistemologies, labor practices, and community relationships through an in-depth qualitative analysis of “Listening Across Divides,” a collaborative project conducted by NPR in the lead-up to the 2024 U.S. election. Drawing on interviews with journalists, editors, and project staff across nine public media stations, the study explores how AI-mediated systems designed to record, organize, and surface themes from facilitated community conversations intersected with engagement-oriented journalism practices. Findings show that AI functioned less as a tool for automation than as an infrastructural layer supporting collective listening and cross-newsroom sense-making. The study demonstrates how technologies associated with efficiency and scale may simultaneously support and reshape slower forms of community-centered journalism rooted in sustained listening. In doing so, the article contributes to scholarship on engagement journalism, AI in newswork, and journalistic knowledge production by conceptualizing AI as a sociotechnical infrastructure for mediated collective sense-making.

trending.title: The AI turn in journalism: Disruption, adaptation, and democratic futures
trending.abstract: In this essay, we argue that, unlike previous changes in digital media technologies over the past few decades, this AI “turn” in journalism forces us to rethink journalism’s identity and its relationship with audiences. While AI complicates and challenges some existing professional, social, political, and economic structures, it also offers new ways to realize desired journalistic objectives that were previously considered to be impractical, if not impossible. Drawing on four orienting ideas—adoption and hype, power and dependency, audiences and democratic implications, and education and empowerment—we unpack the implications of this AI turn in journalism and the consequences for the future of the journalistic field.

trending.title: Journalists as individual users of artificial intelligence: Examining journalists’ “value-motivated use” of ChatGPT and other AI tools within and without the newsroom
trending.abstract: ChatGPT and other AI applications have made the widespread use of artificial intelligence possible with their conversational interfaces and open accessibility – this “mainstreaming” of AI use has become concerning for news organizations as they grapple with the creation of appropriate AI-related guidelines and tools for their newsrooms. Even while such discussions are ongoing, the cultural shift among journalists has already begun. This paper highlights the role of journalists not simply as agents working within the confines of news organizations, but as actors with individual agency to enact change. Their use of AI has already gained significant momentum, with or without newsroom oversight and direction. This paper, supported by field theory, uses in-depth interviews with journalists and editors to uncover how journalists are themselves using AI in their day-to-day work, and how they ensure their values of “good journalism” are not compromised. Results show that journalists are already personally using AI in numerous tasks across all the stages of news production, namely in news gathering, news writing and presentation, news editing, and news promotion, and have three strategies to maintain their practice of “good journalism”. These results prompt the paper’s proposition of a new “value-motivated use” perspective to summarize journalistic adoption of AI – that it is the journalistic values that motivate their increased use of AI, as well as the values that motivate their limitations of this use; journalists will use the technology only to the extent that it aligns with the values of their profession.

trending.title: How social media affordances shape journalistic content production: A stimulus-based interview study on journalists’ perceptions
trending.abstract: Social media platforms are increasingly central for delivering journalistic content. While evidence suggests that social media led to adaptations of journalistic production routines, comparatively little is known about the specific platform characteristics that shape coordinating, selecting, and editing social media content. Adopting an affordance lens, this study seeks to tackle this gap and investigates how social media journalists perceive platform properties and their influence on journalistic contenft production. To answer this question, the study relies on stimulus-based qualitative interviews with 34 social media journalists from Germany, focusing primarily on TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook. By combining platform walkthroughs and reconstruction interviews, the analysis provides fine-grained insights into how a set of affordances, ranging from the perceived degree of algorithmic curation over (user-induced) spatiotemporal boundaries to platforms’ communicative forms, shapes the different stages of content production. The proposed affordances are both universal and variable, forming a typology that facilitates systematic comparisons across current and future platforms.

trending.title: Depictions of Black Americans in U.S. Television News, 1990-2020
trending.abstract: How are Black Americans depicted in U.S. television news? This paper provides an empirical investigation into the news topics in which Black Americans are mentioned, or not mentioned, across nearly the entire population of network television news content from 1990 to 2020. Previous literatures suggest that Black Americans are most likely to appear in stories about (a) crime and violence, (b) poverty and welfare, (c) civil rights and protest, and (d) sports. Based on structural topic modelling of news transcripts, we find broad support for some of these expectations, across a much larger corpus than has been available in prior work. Indeed, we find that Black Americans are most likely to appear in topics such as sports, and criminal violence, and are largely absent from areas such as business and health. Our findings have important implications for the study and practice of journalism, and for our understanding of the nature and effects of racial depictions in U.S. media.

trending.title: AI-reporters as the future of journalism? Investigating recipients’ credibility evaluations of AI-authored news
trending.abstract: AI-authored news articles are becoming increasingly relevant, but little is known about how recipients evaluate news credibility attributed to an AI (artificial intelligence) author compared to a human journalist author. Referring to the machine heuristic ( Sundar, 2008 ) and Expectancy Violations Theory ( Burgoon, 2015 ), this study compared articles with AI-author labels to articles with human-author labels and without author labels. It further included AI trust and attitudinal congruence as relevant aspects to impact credibility evaluations of a news article about cannabis legalization. Based on a 2 (direction of arguments: pro vs contra) x 3 (author label: AI vs human vs none) between-subjects experiment with 844 German respondents, a MANCOVA was conducted. While controlling for people’s attitudinal congruence with the article, we found AI-authored articles’ sources evaluated as less credible than the human-authored articles’ sources, but no significant differences compared to those without author labels. News author labels did not affect message credibility evaluations, and AI trust did not have the expected interaction effect with the author labels. However, it directly affected credibility evaluations of the message and source. Furthermore, attitudinal congruence strongly impacted credibility evaluations. Results are discussed and contextualized regarding theoretical and practical implications.

trending.title: The relationship between news trust, mistrust and audience disengagement
trending.abstract: The global decline of trust in news is a concern for democracy and news organisations. It is often assumed that distrust in news will turn citizens away from it. However, the relationship between trust and news engagement is not straightforward. Those who distrust news may continue to consume it, and those who have high trust in news may choose to disengage from it. This study addresses this puzzling phenomenon by applying the concept of ‘mistrust’ and differentiating it from low or lack of trust. Mistrust is defined as exercising scepticism towards news and deferring trust. Confirmatory factor analysis of an online survey ( n = 4401) conducted in Australia, Singapore and UK between March and April 2023 reveals that trust and mistrust are empirically separate constructs and that they co-exist. Further logistic regression analysis shows that mistrust can lead to news avoidance. This news avoidance does not necessarily mean disengagement from news. Instead, we find low trust is a factor that turns people away from news altogether. By deciphering the complex relationship between trust and mistrust, this study provides new insights into understanding audiences’ disengagement with news.

trending.title: Misinformation, disinformation, and fake news? Proposing a typology framework of false information
trending.abstract: Over the past years, misinformation has attracted considerable attention in communication research. While there is now general agreement on what constitutes misinformation, the applicability of relevant definitions to fact-checking practices, computational fake news detection, and legal sanctions is minimal. More importantly, the definitions do not clarify what contributes to information falsity. This article argues that in clarifying the nature of misinformation, the content’s format, the author’s intent, and opinionated information are less of a concern than the traits used to construct misinformation. To make progress in identifying the causes of fake news, the various traits used to construct misinformation should be considered prior to inferring the author’s intentions, but not vice versa. Based on the findings of existing taxonomies and the labels used to provide conclusions in fact-checking reports, a typology framework is proposed, dividing false information into four main categories: fabrication, manipulation, misinterpretation, and providing incomplete information. Such a framework is anticipated to demonstrate practicality for detecting misinformation online. Given that different kinds of false information have different implied intentions, different implications for fake news detection and governance are expected.

trending.title: Action research at the BBC: Interrogating artificial intelligence with journalists to generate actionable insights for the newsroom
trending.abstract: In this paper, we provide reflections from an embedded action research project undertaken at the UK's largest public service broadcaster, the BBC, over a three-year period. It was aimed at eliciting research insights about the role and understanding of AI in news production and also intervening to engender change in the newsroom. We surface the messy realities of conducting this work, including the challenges to funding such long-term and resource-intensive research and the difficulties of measuring impacts. We include practical guidance to demystify the process of action-oriented research that strives for targeted change in news contexts, highlighting the need for researchers to cost in time for translational work and the importance of having 'critical friends' to hold them to account. Ultimately, we emphasise the value of action research in journalism studies and particularly at the nexus of news and technology. We argue for approaches that retain a critical perspective whilst closing the gap between theory, critique, and practice.

trending.title: A new innovative method to evaluate public news broadcasting: Preserving democracy, culture, and identity during the first AI revolution
trending.abstract: As the first AI revolution rapidly eliminates numerous journalism, reporting, and news writing jobs, the debate over taxpayer-funded public broadcasting entities in some countries gains momentum. The potential threats posed by AI-generated content, unregulated or self-regulated social media, and radical social networking sites to public opinion and election results are concerning. This study presents the first cost-benefit analysis of publicly funded broadcasting, with a focus on the CBC/Radio-Canada. The benefits are estimated using mathematical models via the mass (Canadian Newsstream database) and social media (YouTube). CBC/Radio-Canada has contributed 471,706 newsprints via the news wire, while also generating 126,436 videos across 16 YouTube accounts, with 4,031,467,452 views and 8,065,340 subscribers, resulting in a benefit-to-cost ratio of 2.17 × 10 5 :1. Therefore, CBC/Radio-Canada, as a taxpayer-funded entity, is highly cost-effective and efficient. CBC/Radio-Canada further contributes billions of dollars annually to the local and national economies, while also playing a vital role in preserving the cultures and identities of its many nations, promoting official languages, multiculturalism, tolerance, national cohesion, and international influence, and, most importantly, democracy in an ever-changing world. It is recommended that CBC/Radio-Canada begin offering more Canadian news and content in local, rural, French, Indigenous, Inuit, and other languages.

trending.title: Insulted and outraged: How do Portuguese journalists experience precarity
trending.abstract: Journalism studies’ literature on precarity has mainly focused on job insecurity, job loss, and the increase of atypical work relationships. Several studies report a growing deterioration of journalists’ work conditions worldwide, indicating a precarization of journalism. Precarity may impact journalistic norms and routines, it may contribute to dissatisfaction and loss of quality of life, it may impact journalists’ health and wellbeing, and even the quality of news content. Journalists’ experiences of precarity should, therefore, be explored. This study aims at assessing Portuguese journalists’ perceptions of precarity through semi-structured interviews ( N = 50) followed by a qualitative content analysis. Precarity emerged as one of journalists’ top concerns, and several interviewees classified their incomes as “insulting,” “ridiculous” or “outrageous.” Journalists also worry that precarity may be contributing to a lack of diversity within newsrooms, making the profession “off-limits” to many.

trending.title: When the news comes from a bot: How AI authorship and emotion shape cognitive, affective, and behavioral responses
trending.abstract: AI-generated news is becoming increasingly prevalent on social media, raising questions about how audiences perceive, evaluate, and engage with this content. This study examines how AI authorship labeling (vs. human labeling) and content type (factual, conspiratorial, partisan) jointly shape readers’ cognitive, affective, and behavioral responses. Across three experiments ( N = 1,600), results show that readers could not reliably detect AI authorship without disclosure, although their evaluations nonetheless diverged depending on content type. When content was labeled as “AI-generated,” it consistently received lower cognitive and affective evaluations—regardless of factual accuracy—indicating a robust AI aversion effect. Crucially, emotionally charged content (conspiratorial or partisan) attenuated this effect. Such content elicited stronger engagement and sharing intentions, even when attributed to AI, suggesting that emotional resonance can override source skepticism. These findings support a dual-processing account: while authorship cues shape cognitive judgments, emotional content drives affective and behavioral responses. The results challenge the effectiveness of binary AI transparency labels and underscore the need for context-sensitive disclosure practices in journalism. They also reveal new challenges for platform governance and digital literacy, especially in curbing emotionally manipulative AI-generated content on social media.

trending.title: From disruptive protests to disrupted news frames: Comparing German news on climate protests
trending.abstract: This paper examines how news frames on disruptive climate protests differ from coverage of conventional protests in news outlets with different political leanings. Analyzing 6632 articles from 21 ideologically diverse German news sources between January 2022 and May 2023, we apply Word2Vec for semantic mapping, emotion classifiers, and qualitative evaluations to assess the frames present in the coverage of climate movements, and the anger attached to these frames. Comparing the more disruptive protests of the group “The Last Generation” and the more conventional protest movement “Fridays for Future”, we find that coverage of “Fridays for Future” varies predictably across the ideological spectrum: Right-wing outlets present protesters as extreme or criminal, while other outlets make reference to climate justice within their coverage of the protests, thereby following the movement’s own framing. When covering the more disruptive “Last Generation”, the entire news landscape engages in an emotionally-charged debate, asking whether the protesters are extremists or criminals, while barely discussing their actual demands. Amid an increasingly affectively polarized media debate on disruptive climate protests, left- and right-wing media remain divided in their evaluations of the protests, but focus on criminality and extremism rather than climate justice. The findings should serve as a reminder to journalists of their responsibility to carefully reflect the frames through which they cover protest movements.

trending.title: Too many numbers and worse word choice: Why readers find data-driven news articles produced with automation harder to understand
trending.abstract: The production of data-driven journalism is becoming increasingly automated, impacting its composition and comprehensibility. Given the importance of data-driven reporting for democratic participation, this study investigates, firstly, how readers evaluate the composition of data-driven articles produced with and without the help of automation and, secondly, how these evaluations affect readers’ perceptions of the articles’ comprehensibility. In an online survey experiment, 3135 online news consumers evaluated 24 articles produced with or without automation using criteria developed in prior research. Our factor analysis reduced those criteria to five categories that matter in readers’ evaluations of the articles’ composition: numeric features, writing style, sentence and paragraph length, descriptive language, and word choice. Our results show, firstly, that although the perception of news stories produced with automation did not differ significantly from that of news stories produced without automation regarding sentence and paragraph length and writing style, the stories produced with automation were evaluated as significantly less comprehensible; and, secondly, that this can be explained partly by readers’ perceptions of some of the other article composition categories, which were rated significantly worse in automated articles. Our findings suggest that using automation to produce data-driven news articles changes their perceived composition in ways that negatively impact comprehensibility. However, this study also suggests how such articles could be made more comprehensible. Specifically, when ‘post-editing’ automated articles, journalists should aim to further reduce the quantity of numbers, better explain words that readers are unlikely to understand and change inappropriate wording.

trending.title: “I feel disgusted”: Experiences of moral injury and its impact on the well-being of conflict journalists
trending.abstract: Journalists working in conflict zones are regularly exposed to potentially morally injurious events, which can result in moral injury with a significant negative impact on their psychological well-being. However, as the dialogue around journalist well-being continues to grow, conflict journalists’ experiences of moral injury remain unexplored. This paper seeks to fill this gap by asking the following questions: How do conflict journalists describe their experiences of exposure to potentially morally injurious events? How do conflict journalists perceive the impact of exposure to potentially morally injurious events on their personal and professional well-being? Through 32 in-depth interviews with conflict journalists in Pakistan, we identified four potentially morally injurious events experienced by participant journalists, including failure to be a good witness, interviewing victims of terror events, putting other journalists’ lives in danger, and betrayal by their organizations. Our findings indicate that conflict journalists experience shame, guilt, and self-loathing after exposure to potentially morally injurious events. These experiences also negatively impact their interpersonal relationships, perception of their moral decision-making, and overall job satisfaction. We argue for approaching mental well-being as a systemic issue and offer suggestions for improving mental health literacy among journalists.

trending.title: When words disempower: A computational feminist analysis of dowry narratives in South Asian press
trending.abstract: Although legally prohibited, the dowry system remains a persistent threat to women’s safety and autonomy across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Nepal. This study examines how English language newspapers in these countries frame dowry related news, using a novel computational tool, the Dowry Disempowerment Index (DDI), to measure narrative agency and lexical framing. Drawing on feminist media theories of symbolic annihilation and gendered mediation, the study applies a custom lexicon of victimhood, passivity, and empowerment to over 8000 news articles published between 2004 and 2024. By integrating sentiment polarity and term frequency, the DDI quantifies the extent of disempowerment or resistance encoded in media discourse. Regression analysis reveals that victim and passive language significantly elevate DDI scores, while empowerment terms lower them. Bangladesh and India exhibit the highest narrative disempowerment, while Pakistan demonstrates relatively lower DDI scores, partly due to structural critiques and community based narratives. Nepal’s neutral framing reflects its portrayal of dowry as a social deviation. This research offers a scalable, replicable model for computational feminist media analysis and calls for a shift in journalistic framing to amplify women’s agency and rights in public discourse. The findings hold implications for feminist advocacy and media reform.

trending.title: “Aren’t we all journalists?” Citizen journalism, disinformation and the weaponization of social media in conflict torn Mali
trending.abstract: The study combines domain expertise and computational community detection to uncover what role citizen journalists and social media platforms play in mediating the dynamics of conflict in Mali. Under conditions of the growing conflict in Mali, citizen journalists are opening Twitter (rebranded as X) accounts to stay updated and tweet about the ongoing socio-political tensions, chronicling life in a conflict-ravaged context. This article conceptualizes the rapid reliance on Twitter among citizen journalists consisting of bloggers, activists, government officials and NGO’s as a form of networked conflict and networked journalism. Networked journalism emerges as professional journalists adopt tools and techniques used by nonprofessionals (and vice versa) to gather and disseminate information while networked conflict involves the consequential and intricate relationship between social media and conflict in the Sahel region of Africa. Our findings show that Twitter is a source of action that promotes and mediates conflict, which exposes users to conflict-related content. The findings also show that what accounts for citizen journalism in a conflict setting is vague as those with access to Twitter and as such, the presumed ability to influence the narrative, unequivocally consider themselves citizen journalists.

trending.title: ‘At this point, I have no idea’: Determining a sports journalist in the 2020s
trending.abstract: This study utilizes interviews with 37 full-time, professional sports journalists to understand how they construct their identity. With social identity theory as a framework, the study found that access, organizational backing, and role conception represent characteristics essential to being a sports journalist (the in-group). While the journalists also identified what they considered business reporters, social media personalities, and non-objective analysts as characteristics that, in some cases, exclude persons from calling themselves sports journalists (the out-group). These results are then interpreted through the framework of social identity theory, boundary work and professional identity.

trending.title: Challengers in the journalistic field – A study of alternative media and their relations to incumbents, governance units, the state, and each other
trending.abstract: The interaction between alternative and mainstream media is complex and often contentious. Mainstream journalists question the professionalism and political agendas of alternative media, while the latter criticize mainstream journalists for being biased and elitist. This paper investigates the positioning of alternative media in the journalistic field, both as a collective and as individual entities. Using the Strategic Action Field approach, we take an in-depth look at alternative media as challengers, approaching them as less privileged actors in the journalistic field. Through interviews with editors of alternative media in Norway, we engage with, and not merely discuss, antagonistic and agonistic actors in journalism. The study offers a nuanced understanding of how left-wing and right-wing alternative media, both collectively and individually, relate to other social actors in the field including media organizations (incumbents), press organizations and press councils (governance units), funders (state), and other alternative media (challengers). In the article, we identify three different positions, the anti-systemic, the independent and the pragmatic, pointing to different levels of knowledge of the journalistic field and strategic actions amongst alternative media.

trending.title: Artificial intelligence as a game-changer or passing tech fad in journalism? A qualitative study on journalists’ perceptions and technology adoption in a Global South country
trending.abstract: This study investigates how journalists perceive and adopt artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in their professional routines, offering timely insights into a field undergoing rapid technological change. Drawing on 20 semi-structured interviews with journalists from a range of media organizations in India, this research situates its analysis within the Global South context to explore (1) how journalists make use of AI technologies in their newswork and (2) what factors shape journalists’ adoption behavior toward AI. Acknowledging that individual experiences and contextual factors shape technology adoption, the study adopts a qualitative approach to the Technology Acceptance Model 3 (TAM3) as a guiding framework. The findings show that AI is increasingly used in journalistic communication processes, with its adoption shaped by journalists’ perceptions of its usefulness and ease of use. By combining a well-established technology acceptance framework with qualitative insights, this study contributes to a better understanding of the multifaceted factors influencing AI adoption in journalism.

trending.title: The logics of innovation. Institutional logics and isomorphic pressures in public service media innovation labs in the age of artificial intelligence
trending.abstract: This study explores how Public Service Media (PSM) innovation laboratories navigate a complex institutional environment that simultaneously constrains and demands innovation. Drawing on the concepts of isomorphic pressures and institutional logics, the study investigates strategies used by PSM innovation labs to innovate within institutional constraints. Based on interviews with editorial technologists from three PSM innovation labs in Germany, we identify five institutional logics that enable innovation despite strong normative and coercive pressures: the logics of agility, efficiency, public service, audience, and interdisciplinary collaboration. These logics function as adaptive mechanisms that enable PSM innovation labs to balance the demands of innovation with adherence to norms, regulations, and limited resources. Our findings illustrate how PSMs can manage institutional complexity and sustain innovation within constrained operational environments. Hence, this study offers a dynamic view of isomorphism, where conformity and agency coexist, and where innovation can emerge from within institutional boundaries rather than in opposition to them.

trending.title: Divisions of labor: Why alternative news users seek out mainstream news media in Denmark and how they combine mainstream and alternative content
trending.abstract: Alternative media users have low trust in mainstream media but use them, nonetheless. Departing from this paradox, this study explores why the users seek out mainstream media and how they combine alternative and mainstream content. Qualitative interviews with 25 users of Danish alternative media show that they especially use mainstream news for general orientation but also to fulfil social, opinion, and entertainment needs, as part of everyday habits, and because of unwanted incidental exposure. Furthermore, the study identifies two distinct ways of combining alternative and mainstream media. (1) A clear division of labor where mainstream media provide orientation on current affairs and parts of the picture on topics the users consider biased in mainstream news; and alternative media give counterbalance by providing the missing pieces. (2) An unclear division of labor where alternative and mainstream media play overlapping roles, rendering alternative media less important to the users. The findings suggest that the use of alternative media only makes sense in combination with mainstream news and give little indication that they could entirely displace mainstream media. However, this must be understood in relation to the specific Danish media context and the study concludes by discussing the findings’ relevance in other media contexts. The findings are based on a small sample and cannot be generalized to all Danish users of alternative media.

trending.title: Transformative journalisms and the seductive power of imagery in digital climate niche journalism
trending.abstract: Recent debates around “transformative journalisms” in climate journalism present emerging ways to renegotiate the traditional norm of journalistic objectivity by blurring the boundaries between science, advocacy, and journalism. This paper draws similarity between the seductive powers of journalistic objectivity and of naturalism in news photography, exploring the ways these collide and interact when brought together in the context of image selection and engagement at one niche climate journalism organisation. Using a hybrid ethnographic approach between 2021 and 2023, this research addresses the question of what the engagement with imagery at one specialist climate organisation, Carbon Brief, can tell us about the shifting norms of objectivity and advocacy in climate journalism. Findings explore first the specific understanding of journalistic objectivity being performed by Carbon Brief through their policy-neutral tone, and the multiple ways this is manifest in image use. Second, this paper demonstrates how through their discussions around and engagement with photographic imagery, Carbon Brief are blurring, stretching, and transgressing the boundaries between neutrality and advocacy in climate journalism, as well as the line between naturalism and symbolism in photography. Fundamentally, this paper highlights the contradictory and complex assumptions within both climate journalism’s and news photography’s commitment to versions of objectivity, and argues that transformative journalisms provides a useful concept to understand the plurality, fluidity, and transgression which is often already present at climate-specific journalistic organisations.

trending.title: The truth game: Verification factors behind fact-checkers’ selection decisions
